title: §13-003: Database Integration & High-Performance Endpoints
description: Multiple-choice practice questions and deep runtime verification for §13-003 (Database Integration & High-Performance Endpoints).

cards.concept: Database Integration & High-Performance Endpoints: Fastify Radix Tree & Schema Serialization
cards.question: What core architectural mechanisms allow Fastify to outperform Express in HTTP throughput and latency?

options.text: Fastify is written in Rust and runs outside V8.
Radix tree routing (find-my-way) with O(k) lookup and pre-compiled JSON schema serialization (fast-json-stringify).
Fastify automatically forks an OS process for every incoming request.
Fastify only supports HTTP/3 protocols.

cards.explanation: Fastify uses a radix tree router for O(k) path matching (where k is path length) and compiles JSON response schemas ahead of time using fast-json-stringify, avoiding runtime reflection.
cards.pitfall: Omitting response schemas disables fast-json-stringify optimization, falling back to standard JSON.stringify.

cards.concept: Database Integration & High-Performance Endpoints: HTTP Keep-Alive & Socket Exhaustion
cards.question: Why should backend microservices reuse TCP connections using HTTP Keep-Alive when communicating with internal services?

options.text: It encrypts payloads using hardware TLS.
It avoids the latency and CPU overhead of repeated 3-way TCP handshakes and TLS negotiation, preventing port exhaustion (TIME_WAIT states).
It compresses HTTP headers using Brotli.
It guarantees zero dropped packets over UDP.

cards.explanation: Reusing persistent TCP connections avoids establishing new TCP and TLS handshakes on every request, eliminating port exhaustion caused by sockets lingering in TIME_WAIT.
cards.pitfall: Not setting keep-alive timeouts appropriately can leave idle sockets open indefinitely or cause race conditions when servers close sockets prematurely.
